title: A $10 Light Sensor Could Bring Lab Tests to Your Wrist
summary:
Scientists at the University of Cambridge in England have built a light sensor that costs about $10 but measures as precisely as big laboratory machines. One day, it could help people check their blood sugar without needles.

The device is a spectrometer. A spectrometer studies light that has passed through or bounced off something. Because different materials change light in different ways, the light reveals what a substance is made of. Spectrometers are important in medicine, factories and environmental science, but small ones have usually been less accurate than big ones.

The Cambridge team, working with a start-up company called GlitterinTech, tried a new idea. Instead of splitting light into colors, their sensor uses a math rule called the convolution theorem right on the light itself. "The key insight was to go back to the mathematics," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author. The device is just centimeters across and works in less than a second.

In tests, it correctly identified plastics, medicines, coffee, flour and tea every time. It also measured how much of a substance was mixed into liquids with very high accuracy, beating larger commercial machines in those experiments.

The team also tested it on body measurements, such as skin moisture, blood sugar and other markers, in conditions designed to be like the human body. In one person, they tracked blood sugar over time without piercing the skin. The researchers say more testing is needed before it could become a medical product.

The sensor kept working from minus 20 to 80 degrees Celsius, which could make it useful in wearable devices, factories and outdoor sensors. Professor Qixiang Cheng, who led the project, said it is ready for real-world conditions, not just the lab.
why_it_matters: Cheap, accurate sensors could one day move lab-quality testing into watches and phones, helping with health checks, food safety and environmental monitoring.

background_read: Every material absorbs and reflects light in its own pattern, a bit like a fingerprint, and spectrometers read that pattern to identify substances.
Spectrometers are used in hospitals, factories and labs, but the most accurate ones have usually been large and expensive.
Many people with diabetes must check their blood sugar often, which usually means pricking the skin, so scientists are looking for ways to measure it using light instead.
Making scientific tools smaller and cheaper can let them fit into everyday devices like smartwatches.

└─ SOLUTION: Uses the convolution theorem directly on light
WHO: University of Cambridge and the start-up GlitterinTech; Dr. Chunhui Yao and Prof. Qixiang Cheng

HEALTH TESTS: Measured skin moisture and blood sugar; tracked blood sugar in one person without needles
